package_info.why_malicious: The SNOWLIGHT malware family is a post-exploitation Linux threat designed for remote access, command execution, and credential theft. It is deployed manually or via automated scripts after attackers exploit public-facing application vulnerabilities (such as F5 BIG-IP CVE-2023-46747 or ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709). SNOWLIGHT exhibits advanced behaviors including in-memory payload decryption, fileless execution, privilege escalation, credential harvesting, anti-forensics (file deletion, process masquerading), and persistent command-and-control communication with attacker infrastructure.

execution_context.file_location: Deployed Linux ELF binary (SNOWLIGHT sample, e.g., MD5: 0951109dd1be0d84a33d52c135ba9c97)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes a custom XOR-based loop to decode encrypted payloads in memory, enabling the decryption and subsequent execution of additional malicious code modules.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Custom XOR-based in-memory decoding routines are a hallmark of malware attempting to evade static detection and hinder reverse engineering. The presence of such a loop in a system binary is highly anomalous.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Linux binaries rarely implement custom XOR loops to decrypt large code or data sections at runtime, especially outside of cryptographic or DRM contexts.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may use XOR for lightweight obfuscation of configuration data, but not for large-scale code or payload decryption and execution.
key_indicators: Custom XOR loop in executable code section
YARA rule matches for XOR-based obfuscation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: { BA 01 00 00 00 BE 3B 0B 40 00 BF 3F 01 00 00 E8 8C FE FF FF }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code invokes the memfd_create syscall to generate an anonymous, in-memory file descriptor, writes a secondary payload into this memory region, and executes it directly from memory, enabling fileless execution of malicious code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of memfd_create for fileless, in-memory execution of payloads is a sophisticated anti-forensics and evasion technique, commonly observed in advanced Linux malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not use memfd_create to execute arbitrary code from memory. This behavior is strongly associated with malware seeking to avoid detection and forensic analysis.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some container runtimes or advanced system tools may use memfd_create for legitimate in-memory operations, but not for loading and executing untrusted or arbitrary code.
key_indicators: memfd_create syscall usage in executable code
Absence of dropped files on disk
YARA rule matches for memfd_create-based malware

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
‘–[foreground|fingerprint|proxy|process_name] -d|–destination <server_address>’
‘-d or –destination Server connect back address (can be baked in)’
‘–foreground Causes the client to run without forking to background’
‘–fingerprint Server public key SHA256 hex fingerprint for auth’
‘–proxy Location of HTTP connect proxy to use’
‘–process_name Process name shown in tasklist/process list’
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code parses command-line arguments to configure a reverse shell client, establishes an outbound connection to a specified attacker-controlled C2 server (optionally via proxy), and can spoof its process name in the system process list to evade detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reverse shell clients that connect to attacker infrastructure, support process name spoofing, and allow proxy configuration are classic indicators of backdoor malware designed for covert remote access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not provide reverse shell functionality or allow arbitrary process name spoofing for evasion, especially in production environments.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may implement similar options, but such tools are not expected on production systems and are typically well-documented and controlled.
key_indicators: Hardcoded or user-supplied C2 server addresses
Process name spoofing in process list

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits public-facing application vulnerabilities (e.g., F5 BIG-IP CVE-2023-46747 or ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709) to gain initial access to the target Linux system.
Attacker uploads and executes SNOWLIGHT or GOREVERSE malware binaries on the compromised system to establish a foothold.

Malware decodes and executes additional payloads in memory (using XOR-based decryption and fileless execution), establishes reverse shell connections to attacker C2 infrastructure, and enables remote command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft, lateral movement, and further post-exploitation

attack_chain.action: Malware performs credential theft (e.g., accessing /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow), system discovery, and anti-forensics actions such as file deletion and process masquerading.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of custom XOR-based in-memory decoding routines in Linux ELF binaries
Use of memfd_create syscall for fileless, in-memory payload execution
Reverse shell connections to hardcoded or attacker-controlled C2 addresses
Process name spoofing or masquerading in process list
Command-line arguments enabling reverse shell or proxy configuration (e.g., --destination, --proxy, --process_name)
file_indicators: Linux ELF binaries with MD5 hashes: 0951109dd1be0d84a33d52c135ba9c97, c867881c56698f938b4e8edafe76a09b, df4603548b10211f0aa77d0e9a172438, 0ba435460fb7622344eec28063274b8a, a78bf3d16349eba86719539ee8ef562d
Binaries named or containing 'goreverse', 'snowlight', or similar strings
Unusual executable files in /tmp, /dev/shm, or other world-writable directories
network_indicators: Non-standard protocol traffic indicative of custom C2 or reverse shell activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of unknown or suspicious Linux ELF binaries, especially those exhibiting XOR-based in-memory decoding or invoking memfd_create for fileless execution. Detect outbound connections to known C2 infrastructure (e.g., 172.245.68.110:8888) and monitor for reverse shell behavior, such as unexpected outbound connections, process name spoofing, or command-line arguments indicating reverse shell or proxy configuration. Use YARA rules (e.g., from Mandiant) to scan for SNOWLIGHT and GOREVERSE malware families, and correlate findings with file hashes and network indicators for comprehensive detection.
